title: "What do variance and normality tests establish?"
output: rmarkdown::html_vignette

  %\VignetteIndexEntry{What do variance and normality tests establish?}

Do formal tests support the concerns in a customer-spending residual plot?
We will use the same model as the
[residual diagnostics guide](residual-diagnostics.html), distinguish two
null hypotheses and interpret the results together. Here both the
variance test and normality checks give evidence against their nulls.
They identify questions for further investigation, without choosing a remedy.

## Keep the model and observations fixed

**Example data: wholesale customer spending**

The 440 observations record annual spending in monetary units, with currency unspecified. The earlier plots showed uneven residual spread and departures from normality. Fit the same milk-on-grocery model so that the tests address those findings. See `?wholesale_customers` for the source and licence.

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

```{r model, message=FALSE}
library(olsrr)
customer_data <- wholesale_customers[c("milk", "grocery")]
stopifnot(nrow(customer_data) == 440L, !anyNA(customer_data))
spending_model <- lm(milk ~ grocery, data = customer_data)
```

The assumptions concern unobserved model errors conditional on grocery spending.
The functions use fitted residuals to investigate them. Residuals inherit
constraints and dependence from fitting, so formal distribution tests
applied to them are diagnostic approximations, not a complete validation
of the error model.

## Test a specified variance pattern

The Breusch-Pagan null is **constant conditional error variance**. The
default call looks for variance associated with the model's fitted values.
Its alternative concerns that specified direction; it does not cover every
possible pattern of changing variance. This implementation assumes normal
errors for its reference calibration, as well as an appropriate mean
model and independent observations.

```{r variance-test}
variance_test <- ols_test_breusch_pagan(spending_model)
variance_test
```

The chi-square statistic is 936.089 with one degree of freedom and p < 0.0001.
At a prespecified 5% significance level, that is evidence against the
constant-variance null in the tested direction. It agrees with the visual
concern about widening spread, but does not prove which variance function
is correct. An incorrect mean model can also create a residual pattern.

Changing variance does not by itself make OLS coefficients biased:
unbiasedness requires a correctly specified conditional mean with zero
conditional-mean errors, and consistency needs corresponding exogeneity
and regularity conditions. The usual constant-variance standard errors
can nevertheless be inappropriate, affecting confidence intervals and
tests. A rejected variance test does not invalidate every fitted value
or automatically select weighted fitting, a transformation or another remedy.

## Ask a separate normality question

Each normality check has a **normal-distribution null**, with location
and scale estimated from the data. They emphasize different kinds of
departure and inspect the same residuals, so their results are not four
independent confirmations. The Kolmogorov-Smirnov row uses the Lilliefors
correction for estimating the normal mean and standard deviation.

```{r normality-tests}
normality_tests <- ols_test_normality(spending_model)
normality_tests
```

The Shapiro-Wilk, Lilliefors, Cramer-von Mises and Anderson-Darling p-values are all below 0.0001. These results
indicate departures from a normal shape at a 5% threshold, consistent
with the Q-Q plot's tails. They do not distinguish skewness caused
by changing variance from a missed mean relationship or unusual observations.

A large p-value would mean insufficient evidence against the particular
null, not proof that an assumption holds. Small samples can miss relevant
departures and large samples can detect minor ones. Normality is useful
for exact small-sample inference under the model; it is not necessary
just to compute least-squares coefficients. No test here establishes
independence or the suitability of the model for new customers.

## Keep other test options in context

| Question or option | Function and scope |
|---|---|
| Test variance against model predictors or selected predictors | [`ols_test_breusch_pagan()`](https://olsrr.rsquaredacademy.com/reference/ols_test_breusch_pagan.html) with `rhs = TRUE` or `vars` |
| Test several variance directions | `multiple = TRUE` with `rhs = TRUE`; `p.adj` offers Holm, Bonferroni and Sidak adjustments |
| Explore another variance test | [`ols_test_score()`](https://olsrr.rsquaredacademy.com/reference/ols_test_score.html), [`ols_test_f()`](https://olsrr.rsquaredacademy.com/reference/ols_test_f.html); read their assumptions before use |
| Summarize alignment with normal scores | [`ols_test_correlation()`](https://olsrr.rsquaredacademy.com/reference/ols_test_correlation.html); this is not a serial-correlation diagnostic |

These options change the question or calibration. Do not search among
them for a favorable p-value. The variance and residual-normality
diagnostics used here are not supported for weighted models; consult the
individual function help before extending the example.

### Separate sidebar: compare genuinely grouped variances

**Example data: wholesale customer regions**

Bartlett's test asks whether population variances are equal across groups. Here the question concerns milk spending in Lisbon, Porto and the other regions. This is a separate grouped question, not a replacement test of regression residual variance.

```{r grouped-variance}
ols_test_bartlett(wholesale_customers, "milk", group_var = "region")
```

The statistic is 16.350 on two degrees of freedom, with p = 0.0003. This is evidence against equal group variances. Bartlett's calibration is sensitive to departures from normality and assumes independent observations within and between groups. Inspect the group distributions before relying on it.

Next, revisit the [two residual plots](residual-diagnostics.html) and
investigate the mean shape and spread together. The help pages for

[`ols_test_normality()`](https://olsrr.rsquaredacademy.com/reference/ols_test_normality.html) and
[`ols_test_bartlett()`](https://olsrr.rsquaredacademy.com/reference/ols_test_bartlett.html)
describe their interfaces and limitations. Choose any follow-up model
using the data context and compare its diagnostics on the same rows.
